title: Highly Complex Sentence Architecture
subtitle: C2 academic and literary writing often uses long sentences that nest several subordinate clauses, front entire clauses for emphasis, and pack dense noun phrases…
objectives: Understand and use: Nested subordinate clauses — a main clause can contain a relative clause, which itself contains another clause, building layers of information.
Understand and use: Multi-clause fronting — moving an entire subordinate clause (or more than one) to the front of the sentence for emphasis, cohesion with the previous sentence, or rhythm.
Understand and use: High-density noun phrases and academic phrasing — combining nominalization, multiple modifiers and embedded clauses into a single compact subject or object.

content.intro: C2 academic and literary writing often uses long sentences that nest several subordinate clauses, front entire clauses for emphasis, and pack dense noun phrases — all while remaining grammatically clear.

rules.heading: a) Nested subordinate clauses — a main clause can contain a relative clause, which itself contains another clause, building layers of information.
rules.body: The report, which the committee — most of whom had opposed the original plan — reluctantly approved, outlined a strategy that few believed would work.

rules.heading: b) Multi-clause fronting — moving an entire subordinate clause (or more than one) to the front of the sentence for emphasis, cohesion with the previous sentence, or rhythm.
rules.body:
Although the data seemed conclusive, and although several experts had endorsed the findings, the board remained unconvinced.

What had once seemed an impossible goal, given the constraints they faced, now looked entirely achievable.

rules.heading: c) High-density noun phrases and academic phrasing — combining nominalization, multiple modifiers and embedded clauses into a single compact subject or object.
rules.body:
The steady erosion of public trust in institutions once considered unimpeachable has reshaped modern political discourse.

Key architectural principles at C2:

  • Use dashes or parentheses to insert a clause without breaking the main sentence's flow.
  • Keep the main verb clearly identifiable even in a long sentence — readers should never lose track of the core subject-verb relationship.
  • Balance clause length: extremely long sentences need at least one shorter sentence nearby to maintain readability.

examples: The proposal, which had been debated for months and which several board members privately opposed, was finally approved.
Although the results were promising, and although the funding had already been secured, the project was ultimately shelved.
What had once been dismissed as a fringe theory is now widely accepted within the scientific community.
The gradual decline in voter turnout, a trend observed across most Western democracies, has troubled political scientists for decades.
Having reviewed the evidence — evidence that, incidentally, contradicted the official account — the judge dismissed the case.
That she succeeded despite every obstacle placed in her path is a testament to her resilience.
The very policies designed to protect small businesses have, ironically, made survival harder for many of them.
Whatever conclusions one draws from the data, and however one interprets the underlying trends, the overall pattern remains undeniable.
It was not until the final report was published, months after the initial allegations surfaced, that the full scale of the scandal became clear.
The committee's decision, reached only after weeks of heated debate, satisfied almost no one.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report, which the committee approved it, outlined a new strategy.
commonMistakes.right: The report, which the committee approved, outlined a new strategy.
commonMistakes.why: Don't repeat the object with a redundant pronoun ("it") once a relative pronoun ("which") already fills that role.

commonMistakes.wrong: Although the data seemed conclusive, but the board remained unconvinced.
commonMistakes.right: Although the data seemed conclusive, the board remained unconvinced.
commonMistakes.why: "Although" and "but" cannot both introduce the contrast — choose one.

commonMistakes.wrong: What had once seemed impossible, now looked achievable it.
commonMistakes.right: What had once seemed impossible now looked achievable.
commonMistakes.why: No comma is needed between a fronted "what" clause functioning as the subject and the main verb; and don't add a redundant "it" at the end.

commonMistakes.wrong: The decline in trust, that scholars have studied extensively, reshaped politics.
commonMistakes.right: The decline in trust, which scholars have studied extensively, reshaped politics.
commonMistakes.why: In a non-defining (comma-separated) relative clause, use "which," not "that."

commonMistakes.wrong: Having reviewed the evidence, the case were dismissed by the judge.
commonMistakes.right: Having reviewed the evidence, the judge dismissed the case.
commonMistakes.why: The subject right after a participle clause ("Having reviewed...") must be the one performing that action — here, the judge, not the case.

exercises.title: Gap-fill
exercises.instructions: Gap-fill (choose which, that, or leave blank as appropriate for defining/non-defining clauses)

items.prompt: The theory, ___ was first proposed decades ago, has recently gained new support.
items.explanation: Non-defining relative clause (marked by commas) referring to a thing (“theory”) — always “which,” never “that.”

items.prompt: The report ___ she submitted last week contained several errors. (defining, no comma — leave blank, or use “that”)
items.explanation: In a defining relative clause, the pronoun can be dropped when it's the object of its own clause (“the report she submitted”), or you can keep “that.”

items.prompt: Her argument, ___ few could refute, changed the course of the debate.
items.explanation: Same non-defining pattern: a comma-set-off clause referring to a thing (“argument”) needs “which,” not “that.”

items.prompt: The findings ___ the team published were later called into question. (leave blank, or use “that”)
items.explanation: Same object-relative-pronoun omission as above: “findings” is the object of “published,” so the pronoun is optional (or use “that”).

items.prompt: The policy, ___ had been in place for over a decade, was finally repealed.
items.explanation: Non-defining again — “which” is required here and can never be omitted, whether it's the subject or object of its own clause.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite / Transformation (combine the short sentences into one complex sentence using the technique indicated)

items.prompt: The plan was risky. Everyone knew this. The board approved it anyway. (use a fronted concessive clause)
items.modelAnswer: Although the plan was risky, and everyone knew this, the board approved it anyway.

items.prompt: Trust in institutions has declined. This is a trend across many countries. It worries sociologists. (embed the second sentence as a non-defining relative clause / appositive)
items.modelAnswer: Trust in institutions has declined, a trend observed across many countries, worrying sociologists. (or: ...a trend across many countries that worries sociologists.)

items.prompt: The scientists reviewed the data. The data had been collected over ten years. They reached a surprising conclusion. (use a participle clause + embedded relative clause)
items.modelAnswer: Having reviewed data collected over ten years, the scientists reached a surprising conclusion.

items.prompt: Nobody expected the merger to succeed. It succeeded anyway. This surprised the entire industry. (use a "that" nominal clause as the subject: "That...")
items.modelAnswer: That nobody expected the merger to succeed, and yet it did, surprised the entire industry. (or: That the merger succeeded despite nobody expecting it surprised the entire industry.)

items.incorrect: The proposal, that had taken months to draft, was rejected in minutes.
answer: The proposal, which had taken months to draft, was rejected in minutes.
items.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (set off by commas) need “which” for things, never “that.”

items.incorrect: Although the evidence was strong, but the jury hesitated.
answer: Although the evidence was strong, the jury hesitated.
items.explanation: “Although” already introduces the contrast — don't also add “but”; use one or the other, not both.

items.incorrect: Having finished the analysis, the results were presented by the team.
answer: Having finished the analysis, the team presented the results.
items.explanation: The subject right after a participle clause must be the one performing that action — here, the team, not the results.

items.incorrect: The decline, that experts had predicted for years, finally arrived.
answer: The decline, which experts had predicted for years, finally arrived.
items.explanation: Same rule as above: a comma-separated non-defining clause referring to a thing needs “which,” not “that.”

items.incorrect: What seemed impossible at first, it became routine within months.
answer: What seemed impossible at first became routine within months.
items.explanation: A fronted “what”-clause acting as the subject takes no comma before the main verb, and doesn't need a redundant “it” repeating the subject.

items.incorrect: The scandal, which it destroyed his career, was never fully explained.
answer: The scandal, which destroyed his career, was never fully explained.
items.explanation: Don't repeat the subject with “it” once “which” is already doing that job as the clause's subject.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one long sentence with a nested non-defining relative clause about a topic you know well (e.g., work, a hobby, current events).
items.modelAnswer: My grandmother's recipe book, which she compiled over fifty years and which none of us dared to modify, remains the closest thing our family has to a sacred text.

items.prompt: Write one sentence that fronts a full concessive clause ("Although...") before the main clause.
items.modelAnswer: Although the team had prepared for every possible scenario, the actual crisis unfolded in a way nobody had anticipated.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a "That..." clause functioning as the subject.
items.modelAnswer: That she managed to finish the project alone, without any support from management, says a great deal about her determination.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using a participle clause ("Having + past participle...") followed correctly by its logical subject.
items.modelAnswer: Having spent the entire weekend rehearsing, the cast felt ready for opening night.

summary: a) Nested subordinate clauses — a main clause can contain a relative clause, which itself contains another clause, building layers of information.
b) Multi-clause fronting — moving an entire subordinate clause (or more than one) to the front of the sentence for emphasis, cohesion with the previous sentence, or rhythm.
c) High-density noun phrases and academic phrasing — combining nominalization, multiple modifiers and embedded clauses into a single compact subject or object.
